items.prompt: After Story 13 hid the grade button from Students, why is grading still listed as the top remaining security item?
items.answer: Server Actions are POST endpoints, so hiding a button leaves the endpoint
distractors: Because Story 13's new permission table still has zero call sites
Because zod schemas were written, yet never wired into the Actions
Because the role switcher cookie is readable from client-side JavaScript
items.explanation: C1 is only partially addressed: UI gating was centralised and reads were scoped, but 'Actions still do not re-check permissions — hiding a button does not remove the endpoint.' The actions still do not re-check permissions.

items.prompt: A brand-new student with no graded work appears on the dashboard. What average and risk does the app show, and is that a bug to fix quietly?
items.answer: 100% and Low risk; a deliberate, test-pinned rule needing its own ticket
distractors: 0% and Critical risk; the UI should simply hide students with no grades
No average at all, because the domain rule returns null for no grades
100% and Low risk; a harmless display bug, so patch it in the UI
items.explanation: calculateSectionGrade returns percentage 100 when totalPointsPossible <= 0. It is deliberate ('innocent until proven guilty'), pinned by tests/grades.test.ts, and if changed must change in the domain rule, not the UI.

items.prompt: Two workers try to run the same Queued job at once. How does claimJob make sure only one of them executes it?
items.answer: updateMany with the runnable status in WHERE, and count 1 means owned
distractors: Each worker SELECTs the job first and skips it if its status is Running
A Prisma update by id, which throws an error for the second worker
An in-process mutex wrapped around processQueue in the worker
items.explanation: 'Why a queue is not SELECT then UPDATE, and why updateMany's count is the claim.' The guard lives in the WHERE of the write; `update` by id alone would overwrite another worker's claim.

items.prompt: The repo shipped a 15-table dev.db against a 17-table schema. Why did tsc, next build and 129 unit tests all stay green?
items.answer: Each of those checks reads the schema, which was correct
distractors: The unit tests mocked Prisma, so they never ran a single query
next build skips type checking for the generated Prisma client
The missing tables were only used by pages excluded from the build
items.explanation: 'Nothing caught it... because every one of those checks reads the schema, and the schema was correct. Only starting the app found it.' A green build is not a running application. Only starting the app touched the stale database.

items.prompt: How did the dev.db drift happen, and what was the fix?
items.answer: Merges restored the committed binary; dev.db is now gitignored
distractors: Prisma migrations ran out of order; the fix added a migrations folder
SQLite corrupted the file on Windows; the fix switched to Postgres
The seed script dropped two tables; the fix removed the deleteMany calls
items.explanation: Stories 17 and 18 ran prisma db push, changing the binary, and 'the merge tooling restored it from git every time'. Lesson: 'A generated artefact in version control is a liability.' The database is now rebuilt by db:push plus db:seed.

items.prompt: A student was dropped from a section and now wants back in. Why is re-enrolment rejected as 'already enrolled'?
items.answer: Dropping only sets status Dropped, so the unique row stays and is matched
distractors: Dropping deletes the student record, so the enrollment cannot reference it
The waitlist promotion rule blocks students who dropped in the same term
The enrollment form caches the old enrollment status in local storage
items.explanation: @@unique([studentId, classSectionId]) plus dropStudentAction setting status 'Dropped' plus hasExistingEnrollment via findUnique regardless of status. Still unchanged — and Story 12's promotion now relies on updating that single row. The existence check ignores status.

items.prompt: Attendance is unique on [studentId, classSectionId, date] where date is a DateTime. A new writer passes '2026-05-22T09:00'. What happens?
items.answer: A second row for that day, as only bare YYYY-MM-DD keys share midnight UTC
distractors: The upsert updates the existing row, since the date portion of the key matches
The write is rejected by the unique constraint with a P2002 error
Prisma truncates the time component to midnight before comparing
items.explanation: new Date('2026-05-22') is midnight UTC, so the upsert is idempotent only 'as long as every writer uses a bare YYYY-MM-DD string. Pass a date with a time component and you'll create a duplicate row.'

items.prompt: recordAttendanceAction fails on the 12th student of a 30-student register. What state is left behind?
items.answer: A half-recorded register, since no transaction wraps the loop
distractors: Nothing, because Server Actions run inside an implicit transaction
Only the audit rows, because attendance upserts are deferred to the end
The whole register, because the failing student is just skipped
items.explanation: The action loops with an upsert plus an audit write per student; 'There is no db.$transaction anywhere in the codebase', and B11/B12 remain unchanged. The first students' upserts and audit rows stay.

items.prompt: A support note says 'absence on Monday was excused (doctor's note)'. What did the original orchestrator's keyword matching do with it?
items.answer: It added +10 risk, since 'absence' matches regardless of context
distractors: It ignored the note, because 'excused' cancels the keyword match
It lowered the risk score, because excused absences show engagement
It flagged the note for an advisor to read before any scoring
items.explanation: The keyword list ['absence','fail','struggling','missed','absent','behind','backlog'] matches any note mentioning an absence, 'including a note saying the absence was excused.'

items.prompt: A request arrives with no user cookie at all. Who does getActiveUser() say is acting?
items.answer: The admin account, via a fail-open fallback
distractors: Nobody: it returns null, and the page redirects to sign-in
A read-only guest user created on demand
The last user who switched roles on that machine
items.explanation: When the cookie is missing or points at a deleted user, getActiveUser looks up username 'admin'. Fail-open by default; acceptable only because this is a lab, never a deployment.

items.prompt: A student fails Algebra I but aces three other classes. What does the 'Section Average' risk badge show today?
items.answer: A fine-looking average, because risk badges pool all the student's sections
distractors: A failing average, because the badge reads the student's worst section
Four separate averages, one per section the student is enrolled in
The gradebook's Algebra I average, since Story 7 fixed the badge too
items.explanation: calculateStudentRisk receives submissions pooled across sections; still true for risk badges. Only the Story 7 gradebook is correctly scoped per section.

items.front: EduOps docs claim fields like Enrollment.absences and InterventionPlan.advisorId. What is the rule of thumb?
items.back: prisma/schema.prisma and the code are the source of truth. If a doc says a field exists, grep for it first (absences are counted from Attendance; plans have createdById; the student has advisorId).

items.front: EduOps uses prisma db push with no migrations folder. How do you add a required column to a table with rows, and what must you do after any schema change?
items.back: Add it optional (String?), backfill, then tighten — a required column on a populated table fails to push. Restart npm run dev afterwards or the generated Prisma types stay stale.

items.front: Original EduOps bug B6: what went wrong with dead-lettered jobs, and how did Story 3 fix it?
items.back: The worker dead-lettered at attempts + 1 >= maxAttempts, but the UI retry button was only disabled for Succeeded and Running, so attempts could pass maxAttempts forever. Story 3 added JOB_TRANSITIONS and a shared canRunJob predicate so UI and worker agree.
